{
    "id": "09-agentic-patterns/agent-checkpointing",
    "title": "Agent Checkpointing",
    "category": "09-agentic-patterns",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Persist an agent run as resumable checkpoints — state, memory, pending actions — so a failure or restart continues from a recorded point instead of from scratch.",
    "body": "Agent Checkpointing Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A long agent run that cannot resume is a long agent run that will eventually be repeated. This skill treats the run as a sequence of durable states: after each completed step, the run writes a checkpoint — conversation state, working memory, pending tool calls — and a restart restores the latest one before doing anything else. The design question is granularity: checkpoints cost writes, and restarts cost rework, so the checkpoint cadence is chosen by what re-execution is actually allowed to cost. When to Use Use for long-running or stateful agent work — multi-step plans, sessions holding tool state, pipelines vulnerable to timeout or restart. Do not checkpoint every intermediate token of fast, cheap runs; when re-execution costs less than persistence, the checkpoint is pure overhead. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Conversation, memory, and pending actions to persist | | | | Yes | Checkpoint after every step, on demand, or on a schedule | | | | Yes | Latest checkpoint, or a specific recorded point | Procedure 1. Choose the checkpoint unit — step, tool call, or plan stage — based on what re-execution of that unit is allowed to cost. 2. Serialize complete state, not deltas alone: a checkpoint that needs every prior checkpoint to restore is a chain, not a checkpoint. 3. Write the checkpoint atomically, so a crash mid-write leaves the previous check point intact rather than a torn one. 4. On restart, restore the latest checkpoint first and reconcile with reality — replay tool side effects only where the tool contract allows it. 5. Version the checkpoint schema; a restored run must refuse to continue on a state format it cannot fully interpret. 6. Prune old checkpoints on a retention rule, and record the retention decision so the pruning is explainable later. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Durable run states with timestamps and step markers | | | | The checkpoint a restart continues from | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Torn writes | A crash during checkpoint serialization | Write atomically; keep the previous checkpoint valid | | Delta-only state | Restoring requires the entire history | Serialize complete state per checkpoint | | Stale resume | Restored state disagrees with the world it mutated | Reconcile with external state before continuing | | Unversioned schema | A restored run misreads an old format | Version schemas and refuse unknown formats | | Checkpoint storms | Persisting on every token, starving the work | Choose cadence by re-execution cost | Security and Authority Boundary A checkpoint is a complete, portable copy of agent state — credentials in working memory get persisted with it, so checkpoints must inherit t he encryption and access scope of the run itself, and the pruning policy must respect data-retention obligations, not just disk budgets. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The arXiv paper on human-in-the-loop agent oversight (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657). 2. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework overview (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. {
    "id": "09-agentic-patterns/agent-failure-taxonomy",
    "title": "Agent Failure Taxonomy",
    "category": "09-agentic-patterns",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Classify agent failures into a shared, evidence-based taxonomy — planning, retrieval, reasoning, execution, environment — so fixes land at the right layer.",
    "body": "Agent Failure Taxonomy Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Agents fail in characteristic ways, and a fix aimed at the wrong layer is a fix that did not happen. This skill gives the failures names: a plan that never fit the goal, retrieval that brought back wrong evidence, reasoning that misjoined what it had, execution that fumbled a working plan, environment that changed under the run. Classification comes from traces — where the first wrong step appears — and the taxonomy pays for itself by making postmortems comparable across incidents instead of anecdotal. When to Use Use when reviewing a failed agent run — incident triage, postmortem, quality review — before anyone decides what to change. Do not skip classification and jump to the most recent failure; without a layer verdict, fixes become folklore and the same class recurs. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The observable steps of the failed run | | | | Yes | What the run was supposed to accomplish | | | | Yes | The failure classes and their diagnostic criteria | Procedure 1. Reconstruct the run from its trace: what was asked, what was retrieved, what was decided, what was executed. 2. Locate the first wrong step — the earliest point where the run departed from a path that could still reach the goal. 3. Classify by layer: planning, retrieval, reasoning, execution, or environment, using the criteria of the taxonomy rather than intuition. 4. Distinguish root cause from symptom: a wrong answer is a symptom; the layer that injected the error is the cause. 5. Record the classification with its evidence — the trace excerpt that supports it — so the verdict is reviewable. 6. Aggregate over incidents: recurrence by class is the signal that directs where the next fix budget goes. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Failure class, layer, and supporting trace evidence | | | | Cause, fix target layer, and recurrence tracking | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Layer guessing | Verdicts assigned without trace evidence | Classify from the first wrong step, with excerpts | | Symptom fixes | The visible error fixed, the cause untouched | Separate the root cause layer from the symptom | | Folklore drift | Each postmortem invents new categories | Use one shared taxonomy across incidents | | Single-incident bias | One failure reshapes the whole system | Aggregate recurrence by class before redesigning | | Unclassified residue | Failures that fit no class get skipped | Extend the taxonomy explicitly when a class is missing | Security and Authority Boundary Failure traces contain the data the run touched, including anything sensitive it retrieved or produced: postmortems and classification records must redact secrets at capture time, because a taxonomy entry quoting a credential is a leak with good documentation. Ev idence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of fault tree analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faulttreeanalysis). 2. The OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications project (https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/).     "description": "Pause an agent run at defined checkpoints and route the pending action to a human decision, so consequential steps execute only after an explicit approval.",
    "body": "Approval Gates Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Autonomy is a budget, not a binary. This skill spends it deliberately: the run defines which action classes are safe to execute directly, which require a human decision before they commit, and what information the human needs to decide. A gate is a structured pause — the agent stops, presents the action and its context, and waits; the decision is recorded with the action it authorized, so the audit trail says who allowed what, not just what ran. When to Use Use for irreversible or consequential actions — payments, deletions, production changes, external commitments — and for action classes whose blast radius exceeds a configured threshold. Do not gate trivial, reversible steps; an approval process that fires a hundred times a day trains its approvers to click through without reading. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The pending action awaiting authorization | | | | Yes | Which action classes execute directly and which gate | | | | Yes | What the approver needs to decide — inputs, blast radius, reversibility | Procedure 1. Classify actions up front: which execute without a gate, which need a human, and which are refused outright regardless of approval. 2. Define the gate payload before the run starts — action, arguments, predicted effect, and rollback path — so the pause presents a decision, not a mystery. 3. Stop cleanly: the agent suspends at the gate, persists the pending actio n, and surfaces the decision request to the designated approver. 4. Record the verdict with its provenance — who decided, when, and on what evidence — attached to the action it authorized. 5. Execute the approved action exactly as presented; a modified action re-enters the gate rather than riding an old approval. 6. Feed rejections back into policy: repeated refusals of the same action class mean the classification, not the human, is wrong.     "description": "Rewind an agent run to a prior checkpoint, inspect or modify state, and re-execute from that point while preserving checkpoint identity and separating diagnostic forks from production runs.",
    "body": "Time-travel Debugging Description Time-travel debugging replays a stateful agent graph from a recorded checkpoint instead of repeating earlier work. A checkpointer is required to inspect history. State edits create a diagnostic fork and should not silently mutate the original production run. The exact checkpoint API depends on the graph runtime; the example below uses the LangGraph interface already described by this skill. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | graph runtime | Compiled stateful graph with a configured checkpointer | | | | Identifier for the run history | | | | Existing checkpoint identifier | | | | Optional controlled state patch | | Output | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | iterable | Ordered checkpoint snapshots | | | runtime-defined | Result of execution from the selected checkpoint | | | mapping | Configuration identifying the diagnostic replay context | Reference Workflow Diagnostic Protocol 1. Capture the production and checkpoint identifier. 2. Verify that the checkpoint exists before replaying. 3. Replay the unmodified checkpoint first to establish a baseline. 4. Create a separate diagnostic thread before mutating state. 5. Record the state patch and reason for the fork. 6. Compare the forked result with the baseline. 7. Never overwrite production state merely to make a test pass. Failure Modes | Cause | Symptom | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | No checkpointer | Empty history | Configure persistent or test checkpointer before execution | | Checkpoint deleted | History unavailable | Retain checkpoints required by the operational debugging policy | | Invalid state patch | Downstream node failure | Validate state schema before | | Fork shares production identity | Production history is mutated | Use a distinct diagnostic | | Non-deterministic external tool | Replay diverges | Stub or record external effects when reproducibility matters | Reproducibility Limits Checkpoint replay restores graph state, not the external world. HTTP responses, clocks, random seeds, model outputs, databases, and tool side effects can differ unless captured or stubbed. A replay should therefore report which external inputs were restored and which were live. Validation Rules - The target checkpoint must exist before replay. - Diagnostic state changes must use a distinct run identity. - State patches must conform to the graph's state contract. - Replay results must not be presented as identical to production unless external effects were controlled. - Checkpoint identifiers and state changes should be recorded for auditability. Security Boundaries Checkpoint state ca n contain prompts, tool arguments, secrets, or user data. Do not expose checkpoint contents to unauthorized users, logs, or model prompts merely for debugging convenience. State patches must not be allowed to bypass authorization or approval gates. Provenance The workflow is runtime-specific at the API boundary and intentionally does not pin a LangGraph release here. The conceptual guarantees are checkpoint lookup, controlled state replay, and diagnostic isolation; verify exact runtime APIs against the deployed version.     "body": "Tool Invention Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An agent that only uses the tools it was given stalls the first time a task needs a missing primitive. Tool invention closes that gap deliberately: confirm the gap is real, write a minimal contract, implement with tests, validate on held-out cases, and register the tool for reuse. The discipline is what separates invention from improvisation — an invented tool is a durable artifact, not a one-off hack. When to Use Use when a repeated workaround shows a missing primitive: the same task fails or degrades across sessions and no registered tool covers it. Do not invent tools to bypass an existing restriction; a guardrail that blocks a capability is a boundary, not a gap. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The recurring task that exposes the gap | | | | Yes | Existing tools with their contracts | | | | Yes | Failing runs or workarounds that show the gap | Procedure 1. Confirm the gap: search the tool registry and prove no existing tool fits, citing the failure evidence. 2. Write a minimal contract: purpose, typed inputs and outputs, failure modes, and authority requirements. 3. Implement the smallest tool that satisfies the contract; nothing speculative. 4. Test against representative cases plus held-out cases the contract implies but the task did not show. 5. Review the tool (critic pass or second review) for correctness and boundary violations before first use. 6. Register the tool with a version and changelog; retire it when usage ends. They must pass the same permission checks as pre-registered tools, must not wrap prohibited capabilities, and must be registered with their authority requirements declared.
